title: Early Humans and Beginning of Civilisation

topics.title: Early humans: from hunter-gatherers to the first artists

learn.hook: Thousands of years ago, someone in a rock shelter in Madhya Pradesh dipped a finger in red colour and painted a running animal. Those paintings at Bhimbetka still survive!
points: Humans evolved over a very long time. Several human species once existed, such as Homo erectus and the Neanderthals, but Homo sapiens (modern humans) is the only human species living today.
Homo erectus made handaxes and cleavers and was among the early humans to spread out of Africa into Asia and Europe. Over time, skulls became larger and rounder and jaws and teeth became smaller.
Palaeolithic (Old Stone Age) people were hunter-gatherers: they hunted animals, gathered wild plants, moved in search of food and water, and lived in caves, rock shelters or temporary camps.
In the Mesolithic (Middle Stone Age), people used microliths: tiny stone tools often fitted into wooden or bone handles to make arrows, spears and sickles.

Before writing, people communicated through speech, gestures, body decoration, engravings and paintings. The rock shelters of Bhimbetka in Madhya Pradesh, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, preserve such early art.

example.q: Think it through: Archaeologists find a cave with ash, animal bones and many small stone blades. What can they infer about the people who lived there?
steps: Ash suggests the people used fire, for warmth, light, cooking or keeping animals away.
Animal bones suggest they hunted animals for food.
Small stone blades (microliths) suggest they made fine tools, probably fixed into handles.
Since there are no farm tools or houses, they were probably hunter-gatherers who used the cave as a shelter.
example.answer: They were probably Stone Age hunter-gatherers who used fire, hunted animals and made microlith tools.

learn.reallife: When you visit a museum and see a stone handaxe behind glass, remember that someone shaped it carefully by striking one stone with another.

games.title: Which Stone Age period?
items: Mainly hunting and gathering, living in caves
Hunting, fishing and gathering with tiny blades

games.title: Early humans: true or false?
items: Homo sapiens is the only human species living today.
Other human species such as the Neanderthals died out long ago.
Palaeolithic people lived mainly by farming in permanent villages.
Palaeolithic people were hunter-gatherers. Farming villages came in the Neolithic period.
Microliths are very small stone tools.
Bhimbetka rock shelters are in Madhya Pradesh.
Bhimbetka lies in Madhya Pradesh and is famous for its rock paintings.
Writing existed long before humans began to paint on rocks.
Rock art is far older. Writing developed much later, in early civilisations.
Fossils can be preserved remains or impressions of ancient living things.
Fossils help scientists study early humans and animals.

quiz.q: Which is the only human species living today?
quiz.explain: All people alive today belong to Homo sapiens. The other species died out.
quiz.mistake: Thinks older human species still survive

quiz.q: How did Palaeolithic people mainly get their food?
options: By hunting animals and gathering wild plants
quiz.explain: Palaeolithic people were hunter-gatherers who depended directly on nature for food.
quiz.mistake: Places farming too early in human history

quiz.q: What are microliths?
options: Tiny stone tools often fitted into handles
quiz.explain: Microliths are small stone blades and points, typical of the Mesolithic period, often fixed into wooden or bone handles.
quiz.mistake: Does not break the word into micro (small) and lith (stone)

quiz.q: The Bhimbetka rock shelters are famous mainly for
quiz.explain: Bhimbetka in Madhya Pradesh preserves rock paintings made by early people.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up Stone Age sites with later civilisation sites

quiz.q: Which early human species is linked with handaxes and cleavers and with early movement out of Africa?
options: None of the early humans made tools
quiz.explain: Homo erectus made handaxes and cleavers and spread from Africa into Asia and Europe.
quiz.mistake: Does not link tool types with particular human species

quiz.q: How did people communicate before writing was invented?
options: Through speech, gestures, paintings and body decoration
They could not communicate at all
quiz.explain: Spoken language, gestures, rock art, engravings and body decoration were ways of sharing ideas before writing.
quiz.mistake: Thinks communication began only with writing

quiz.q: Why did early humans keep moving from place to place?
options: To search for food and water as seasons and animals moved
quiz.explain: Hunter-gatherers followed animals, ripening plants and water sources, so they moved with the seasons.
quiz.mistake: Imagines later institutions like kings or temples in the Stone Age

quiz.q: Archaeologists make copies of ancient stone tools and use them to cut meat. Why?
options: To test how the tools were made and used
To replace the originals in museums secretly
To prove that tools were never used
quiz.explain: Using replicas helps archaeologists understand how early people made and used their tools.
quiz.mistake: Does not see experiments as a way of studying the past

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Did the very first humans live in houses and buy food from shops like we do? How did they live?'
teach.praise: So early humans hunted and gathered food, made stone tools and lived in caves and rock shelters, moving with the seasons. Amazing!
teach.nudge: Good! But how did they get food, and what did they use as tools?

topics.title: The Neolithic revolution: farming and settled life

learn.hook: Imagine never having to chase your dinner again! When people learned to grow wheat and barley and keep goats, life changed forever.
points: The Neolithic (New Stone Age) brought a great change called the Neolithic revolution: people began growing crops and taming (domesticating) animals such as cattle, sheep and goats.
Farming meant people stayed near their fields, so they built permanent houses and villages. They used polished stone tools, made pottery to store grain and began weaving cloth.
Mehrgarh, in present-day Balochistan (Pakistan), is one of the earliest farming villages in South Asia. People there grew wheat and barley, kept animals and built mud-brick houses and storage rooms.

Extra food (surplus) could be stored, so some people could become potters, weavers or other specialists. Settled life also brought new problems such as crop failure and the need to protect stored grain.
In the Chalcolithic (Copper-Stone) age, people used copper along with stone. Later, people learned to make bronze, a mixture of copper and tin, which gave the Bronze Age its name.

example.q: Think it through: Why did farming lead people to make pottery?
steps: Farmers harvested more grain than they could eat at once.
The surplus had to be stored safely away from damp, insects and rats.
Clay pots could store grain, water and oil, and could also be used for cooking.
Since people now stayed in one place, heavy pots were not a burden to carry around.
example.answer: Settled farmers needed containers to store and cook their surplus food, so pottery became important.

learn.reallife: The earthen matka that keeps water cool in many Indian homes in summer is part of a pottery tradition that began with the first farmers.

quiz.q: What was the most important change of the Neolithic revolution?
options: People began farming and domesticating animals
quiz.explain: The Neolithic revolution was the shift from hunting and gathering to farming and herding.
quiz.mistake: Does not know what made the Neolithic period special

quiz.q: Mehrgarh, one of the earliest farming villages in South Asia, is located in
quiz.explain: Mehrgarh lies in Balochistan, in present-day Pakistan, near the Bolan Pass.
quiz.mistake: Confuses Mehrgarh with sites in other parts of the subcontinent

quiz.q: Which crops were grown at Mehrgarh?
quiz.explain: Remains of wheat and barley have been found at Mehrgarh.
quiz.mistake: Chooses crops that came to India much later, such as potato and maize

quiz.q: Why did farming lead to permanent villages?
options: Because farmers had to stay near their fields and look after crops
Because kings ordered people to stop moving
Because there were no more animals to hunt anywhere
quiz.explain: Crops take months to grow and need care, so farmers settled near their fields.
quiz.mistake: Gives an unrelated or later cause for settled life

quiz.q: Which type of stone tools is typical of the Neolithic period?
quiz.explain: Neolithic people ground and polished their stone tools, making them smoother and sharper.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the tools of different Stone Age periods

quiz.q: How did surplus food change society?
options: Some people could become craftspeople such as potters and weavers
quiz.explain: When farmers produced extra food, others could be fed while they specialised in crafts.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect surplus with specialised occupations

quiz.q: The Chalcolithic age is so called because people used
quiz.explain: Chalco means copper and lithic means stone, so it is the Copper-Stone age.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the meaning of the word Chalcolithic

quiz.q: Which was a new problem faced by settled farming communities?
options: Crop failure and protecting stored grain
quiz.explain: Settled farmers depended on harvests, so a failed crop or stolen grain could cause hunger.
quiz.mistake: Imagines modern problems in ancient times

teach.ask: Gappu chirps: 'Why is it called a revolution? Did people fight a big battle in the Neolithic age?'
teach.praise: No battle! The revolution was farming and taming animals, which let people settle in villages. What a big change!
teach.nudge: Not a battle at all! What new way of getting food began, and how did it change where people lived?

learn.hook: More than 4,000 years ago, cities in north-western India had straight streets, covered drains and standard weights. Town planners today still admire them!
points: The Harappan civilisation, also called the Indus or Sindhu-Sarasvati civilisation, was a Bronze Age civilisation. Its mature, urban phase is dated to about 2600-1900 BCE.
Important sites include Harappa and Mohenjo-daro (now in Pakistan), and Dholavira and Lothal (Gujarat), Kalibangan (Rajasthan) and Rakhigarhi (Haryana) in India.

Cities were planned with streets meeting at right angles, houses of baked bricks of standard proportions and covered drains. Mohenjo-daro had the Great Bath, Dholavira had large water reservoirs and Lothal had a dockyard.

Harappans used standard cubical stone weights. Smaller weights followed a doubling pattern (1, 2, 4, 8, 16...) and larger ones used multiples of ten. Kalibangan shows a ploughed field with criss-cross furrows.
They traded with Mesopotamia, whose records probably called the region 'Meluhha'. The Harappan script, found on seals and pots, has not yet been deciphered.

example.q: Think it through: Why have scholars still not been able to read the Harappan script?
steps: Most inscriptions are very short, often only a few signs on a seal.
No bilingual inscription has been found, like the Rosetta Stone that gave the same text in known and unknown scripts.
We do not know for certain which language the Harappans spoke.
Without longer texts or a key, scholars cannot confidently match signs to sounds or words.
example.answer: The inscriptions are short and there is no bilingual 'key', so the script remains undeciphered.

learn.reallife: Dholavira in the Rann of Kutch became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2021, and visitors can still see its stone reservoirs built to save rainwater.

quiz.q: In which present-day state of India is Dholavira located?
quiz.explain: Dholavira is in the Rann of Kutch in Gujarat.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the states of different Harappan sites

quiz.q: The Great Bath was found at
quiz.explain: The Great Bath, a large brick-lined tank, is one of the best-known structures of Mohenjo-daro.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the special structures of different sites

quiz.q: Which feature shows that Harappan cities were well planned?
options: Streets at right angles and covered drains
quiz.explain: Grid-like streets, baked-brick houses and covered drains show careful town planning.
quiz.mistake: Does not recall the planning features of Harappan towns

quiz.q: Harappan smaller weights followed the pattern 1, 2, 4, 8, ... What is the next weight in this pattern?
quiz.explain: Each weight doubles the previous one, so after 8 comes 16.
quiz.mistake: Adds a fixed number instead of doubling

quiz.q: What did Mesopotamian records probably call the Harappan region?
quiz.explain: Mesopotamian texts mention trade with 'Meluhha', which scholars generally identify with the Harappan region.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up ancient place names from different regions

quiz.q: Why is the Harappan script still a mystery?
options: No Harappan writing has ever been found
Inscriptions are short and no bilingual key has been found
It was banned by later kings
quiz.explain: Thousands of short inscriptions exist, but without a bilingual text the signs cannot be confidently read.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the script is unread because no writing survives

quiz.q: Which Harappan site in Gujarat is known for its dockyard?
quiz.explain: Lothal had a large brick basin that many archaeologists identify as a dockyard for boats.
quiz.mistake: Does not link Lothal with sea trade

quiz.q: The Harappan civilisation is called a Bronze Age civilisation because
options: its people used bronze, an alloy of copper and tin, for tools and objects
it had no metals at all
its buildings were made of bronze
quiz.explain: Harappans made tools, vessels and figures of bronze, which marks the Bronze Age.
quiz.mistake: Thinks bronze was used for buildings, or mixes up bronze and iron

teach.ask: Gappu flaps his wings: 'People say the Harappan cities were super smart. What was so special about them?'
teach.praise: Planned streets, covered drains, standard bricks and weights, and trade with faraway lands. Those cities really were smart!
teach.nudge: Think about how the streets and drains were made, and what helped traders measure goods fairly.

topics.title: Egypt, Mesopotamia and China: river civilisations

learn.hook: Why did so many early civilisations grow beside great rivers? Think of the Nile, the Tigris and Euphrates, and the Huang He: water, fertile soil and boats!
points: Egypt grew along the Nile. Its yearly floods left fertile mud for farming. Rulers called pharaohs were very powerful; huge pyramids, such as the Great Pyramid of Giza, were built as royal tombs.

Egyptians believed in life after death and preserved bodies by mummification. They wrote in hieroglyphics on papyrus; the Rosetta Stone, carrying the same text in hieroglyphic, Demotic and Greek, helped scholars decipher it.

Mesopotamia means 'the land between the rivers' (the Tigris and the Euphrates, in present-day Iraq). Sumerians lived in city-states, built stepped temples called ziggurats and wrote in cuneiform, wedge-shaped marks pressed into clay.
King Hammurabi of Babylon issued a famous code of laws; punishments often depended on a person's social status. The Epic of Gilgamesh is one of the world's oldest stories.

Chinese civilisation grew along the Huang He (Yellow River). Shang rulers used oracle bones, heating bones or shells and reading the cracks, to seek answers about the future. Chinese writing is logographic and the Chinese learned to make silk.

example.q: Think it through: What did the Harappan, Egyptian, Mesopotamian and Chinese civilisations have in common?
steps: All grew in river valleys with water and fertile soil for farming.
Farm surplus supported cities, specialised crafts and trade.
Each developed a form of writing: Harappan script, hieroglyphics, cuneiform and Chinese characters.
Each had organised government and used bronze.
example.answer: River valleys, farming surplus, cities, crafts, trade, writing, organised government and bronze technology.

learn.reallife: Rivers still shape where people live: think of how many Indian cities, such as Varanasi, Patna and Kolkata, stand on the banks of the Ganga or its branches.

games.title: Match the river to the civilisation

quiz.q: What does 'Mesopotamia' mean?
quiz.explain: Mesopotamia lay between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, which is what its Greek name means.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the features of Egypt, China and Mesopotamia

quiz.q: Cuneiform writing was made by
options: pressing wedge-shaped marks into soft clay
quiz.explain: Scribes pressed a reed stylus into wet clay tablets, making wedge-shaped marks.
quiz.mistake: Confuses cuneiform with other ancient writing materials

quiz.q: Which object helped scholars decipher Egyptian hieroglyphics?
quiz.explain: The Rosetta Stone had the same text in hieroglyphic, Demotic and Greek; the known Greek helped decode the others.
quiz.mistake: Does not know how hieroglyphics were deciphered

quiz.q: Why were the Nile floods important to Egyptian farmers?
options: They destroyed all crops every year
They brought gold to the fields
They left fertile mud on the riverbanks
quiz.explain: After the floods went down, rich silt was left behind, making the soil good for crops.
quiz.mistake: Sees floods only as destructive

quiz.q: What were oracle bones used for in ancient China?
options: Seeking answers about the future by reading cracks
quiz.explain: Bones or shells were heated and the cracks were interpreted as answers to questions, a practice called divination.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the purpose of oracle bones

quiz.q: The Code of Hammurabi was a set of
options: laws issued by a king of Babylon
quiz.explain: Hammurabi, king of Babylon in Mesopotamia, issued a written code of laws.
quiz.mistake: Links Hammurabi with the wrong civilisation

quiz.q: Along which river did early Chinese civilisation develop?
quiz.explain: Early Chinese civilisation grew along the Huang He, also called the Yellow River.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the rivers of different civilisations

quiz.q: Why did Egyptians mummify the bodies of the dead?
options: To use them as building material
Because they believed in life after death
quiz.explain: Egyptians believed the dead continued to exist in another life, so they preserved bodies carefully.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect mummification with Egyptian beliefs

teach.ask: Gappu wonders: 'Egypt, Mesopotamia, China... Why did all these old civilisations start near rivers? Couldn't they start on a mountain top?'
teach.praise: Rivers gave water, fertile soil for farming and a way to travel and trade. No wonder cities grew there!
teach.nudge: What did rivers give the farmers, and how did rivers help people move goods?
